mammal_niches_top.name: Mammal guard-hair scale casts & hair atlases (wildlife forensics)
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: The Texas atlas alone covers 150+ species with SEM scale images; ZSI Kolkata, FBI/USFWS-style labs and Brunner & Coman built parallel atlases on three continents that cite different standards.
keywords: guard hair scale cast identification atlas
mammal hair atlas SEM scale pattern

fidelity_card.RAW: Cuticular scale casts (gelatin/cellulose impressions), SEM surface images and photomicrographs in forensic hair atlases
fidelity_card.UNIT: One hair — 150+ species in the Texas atlas, 100+ in the Indian and Australian atlases, one cast-and-mount protocol per atlas tradition
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Species called from scale cast vs DNA barcoding of the same hair/specimen (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: Museum-vouchered hairs (atlas specimens tied to skins/skulls)

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: A single guard hair carries a scale pattern like a fingerprint — forensic atlases were built continent by continent and never checked against each other.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Hair ID is a forensic service literature: regional atlases (Texas 2009, ZSI series, Brunner & Coman 1974) each keyed their own fauna with their own scale vocabulary.

mammal_niches_top.name: Koala fingerprint collections
mammal_niches_top.family: A. Skin prints — fingers, palms, pads & noses
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Headline is perfect and verified (Henneberg 1997), but the known print population is small — one species, tens of documented individuals — so archive depth caps the score.

fidelity_card.RAW: Ink prints and SEM fingertip images from wildlife-park and university anatomy collections
fidelity_card.UNIT: One fingertip — one species, tens of individuals in the published study, unknown numbers in zoo/wildlife-park files, one ink-print protocol
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Koala ridge pattern vs human prints in the same forensic reference files (the second ruler is our own fingerprint system)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: The 1997 Adelaide reference prints (Henneberg, Lambert & Leigh)

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: A koala's fingerprint is nearly indistinguishable from a human's under a microscope — verified in 1997, and no, it has never actually turned up at a crime scene.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: One famous study, then near-silence: wildlife parks handle koalas daily and no print collection was ever built on the 1997 foundation.

mammal_niches_top.name: Dog nose-print archives
mammal_niches_top.family: A. Skin prints — fingers, palms, pads & noses
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Petersen took 350+ animal nose prints in 1922; kennel clubs and insurers ran nose-print registries for decades — paper archives, modern apps are rebuilding from zero.

fidelity_card.RAW: Ink nose prints on index cards and nose photographs in kennel-club, insurer and lab collections
fidelity_card.UNIT: One nose — registries ran to thousands of dogs; the 2021 viability study re-proved uniqueness on 70 dogs / 19 breeds, one ink-or-camera protocol per era
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Nose pattern ID vs microchip/tag records for the same dogs (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: Longitudinal re-prints of the same dog months apart (pattern invariance series)

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: Your dog's nose print is its fingerprint — kennel clubs were filing them on index cards a century ago.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Historic nose-print registries were paper and breed-club local; the smartphone-era startups each built tiny private datasets and none inherited the card archives.

mammal_niches_top.name: Plaster track-cast museum collections
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Museums hold drawers of plaster paw casts — snow leopard, wolf, lynx — made when casts were the data; catalogued as objects, never measured as a set.

fidelity_card.RAW: Plaster and latex track casts with specimen labels in natural-history museum collections
fidelity_card.UNIT: One cast — hundreds per large collection, dozens of species, one cast-making tradition across a century
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Species/sex on the cast label vs the cast re-measured today against FIT-style morphometrics (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: Casts tied to collected specimens or known zoo animals

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: Before cameras, scientists carried plaster to the snow and poured the footprint itself — museums still hold the drawers of poured paws.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Cast collections were catalogued by accession, not by measurement; nobody has run a single morphometric pass across a museum's cast drawers.

mammal_niches_top.name: Elephant footprint age-estimation archives
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Forefoot circumference converts to shoulder height and age; the calibration sets (known-age Amboseli elephants walking in sand) are small, old and priceless.

fidelity_card.RAW: Footprint photographs and forefoot-circumference measurement sheets from known-age elephant studies and ranger monitoring
fidelity_card.UNIT: One footprint — calibration series from known-age individuals (Amboseli), monitoring trails by the thousand across Africa/Asia
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Age read from the footprint vs the elephant's known birth year in the long-term ID catalogues (second ruler)

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: You can read an elephant's age off the print its front foot leaves in the dust — if you have the calibration walks, and almost nobody kept them.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: The method is used by rangers everywhere; the underlying known-age measurement series live in a few theses and project files from the 1980s–2000s.

mammal_niches_top.name: Right-whale head callosity catalogues
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: The callosity pattern is read from aerial photos since the 1970s; the North Atlantic consortium catalogue is curated but the southern-hemisphere catalogues (Argentina, South Africa, Australia) grew separately.

fidelity_card.RAW: Aerial and boat photographs of head callosity patterns in consortium and regional catalogues
fidelity_card.UNIT: One head — ~400 living North Atlantic individuals, thousands in southern catalogues, aerial-photo protocol since Payne's 1970s work
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Callosity ID vs genetic profiles from biopsy of the same whales (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: The North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium catalogue as the curated anchor

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: The rough white patches on a right whale's head are as fixed as a face — whale watchers have read them from planes since the seventies.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Three ocean basins built three callosity catalogues in three institutions; cross-basin matching (whales do cross) rests on personal correspondence, not a joined archive.

mammal_niches_top.name: Manatee scar & tail photo-ID system archives
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Florida's MIPS system has matched manatees by scars/tail notches since the 1970s — a state-run pattern archive with sketch-era roots, mirrored by separate Caribbean/Brazil sets.

fidelity_card.RAW: Underwater photographs and hand-drawn scar sketches in the Manatee Photo-ID System and sister programmes
fidelity_card.UNIT: One manatee — thousands of individuals in Florida alone since the 1970s, sketch-then-photo protocol
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Scar-pattern ID vs PIT-tag/genetic identity recorded at rescue/health assessments (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: Rescued manatees whose identity is known absolutely at release

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: A manatee is known by its propeller scars — the state of Florida keeps a mugshot file, part sketchbook, part database.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: MIPS is an agency system with restricted doors; the sketch-era archive and the non-Florida programmes were never part of any public pattern set.

mammal_niches_top.name: Rhino ear-notch & horn-profile ID records
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Distinct from the landed rhino forearm work: this is the applied ID system — ear notches cut by managers plus horn silhouette profiles, kept per-reserve in sighting books. (Forearm centroid work excluded.)
keywords: rhino sighting book ear notch archive

fidelity_card.RAW: Ear-notch diagrams, horn-profile photographs and sighting-book pages from reserves and rhino monitoring programmes
fidelity_card.UNIT: One rhino — hundreds per reserve, thousands across programmes, notch-code + profile-photo protocol
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Notch/horn ID vs DNA from ear-tissue taken at the notching itself, and horn DNA (RhODIS) (second rulers)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: RhODIS forensic horn-DNA database as the cross-check anchor

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: Rhino managers cut a code into the ear and read the horn's silhouette like a skyline — each reserve keeps its own skyline book.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Ear-notching is universal practice and per-reserve paperwork; horn profiles accumulate in monitoring photos that no cross-reserve system ingests.

mammal_niches_top.name: Pinniped pelage-pattern photo-ID (ringed & monk seals)
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Saimaa's SealID set (57 seals, 2,080 images) proved a pelage dataset can be published — and exposed how many seal colonies still match patterns by eye from slide boxes.

fidelity_card.RAW: Seal flank photographs (slides, then digital) in colony photo-ID catalogues
fidelity_card.UNIT: One flank pattern — hundreds of individuals per colony catalogue (Saimaa ~400 animals; Cap Blanc monk seals since 1993), haul-out photo protocol
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Pelage ID vs flipper-tag / telemetry identity of the same seal (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: SealID's expert-matched public benchmark set (57 individuals, 2,080 images)

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: A ringed seal wears a fingerprint made of rings over its whole body — no two seals have ever worn the same one.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Each seal colony's catalogue belongs to its research group; slide-era catalogues (monk seals 1990s) predate the ML datasets and were never digitised into them.

mammal_niches_top.name: Tiger stripe-pattern camera-trap catalogues
mammal_niches_top.family: D. Coat patterns — stripes, rosettes, spots & scales
mammal_niches_top.score_justification: Every tiger's stripes are mapped by camera traps nationally, but the catalogues are security-sealed per country/programme; the pattern data behind published counts is the stranded layer.
keywords: camera trap tiger individual identification data

fidelity_card.RAW: Camera-trap flank photographs and stripe-matching files in national and NGO tiger programmes
fidelity_card.UNIT: One flank — thousands of individuals across range countries, standard paired-camera protocol
fidelity_card.LABEL_GAP: Stripe ID vs genetic ID from scat collected in the same grids (second ruler)
fidelity_card.ANCHOR: India's national tiger estimation archive as the (restricted) anchor set

mammal_niches_top.headline_shape: No two tigers share a stripe map — countries count their tigers from stripe photographs and then lock the photographs away.
mammal_niches_top.why_niche: Counts are published, pattern files are not; each programme's catalogue is a silo justified by poaching risk, so cross-border tigers are matched by personal contact.
